entries.title: Berlin Airport briefly suspends flights over drone sighting
entries.summary: Airspace over the German capital was temporarily closed after a drone was spotted on the runway. Flights have resumed but are experiencing delays.
entries.content:
Germany

Berlin Airport briefly suspends flights over drone sighting

September 23, 2026

Airspace over the German capital was temporarily closed after a drone was spotted on the runway. Flights have resumed but are experiencing delays.

Berlin's airport briefly suspended flights on Wednesday evening after a drone sighting, Germany's DPA news agency cited airport and police officials as saying.

A drone was spotted on the Berlin Brandenburg Airport's northern runway at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT). Airspace above the airport was closed minutes later and operations were suspended for at least 45 minutes.

Several flights were diverted to Dresden.

As of 9:05 p.m., airspace was reopened but flights were experiencing delays.

Drone sightings on the rise

Drone sightings have become a common occurrence for airports in Europe, with Berlin's airport recording the highest number of sightings in Germany in the first part of the year.

Some 28 drone sightings were recorded during the first six months, as per figures by the German air traffic control (DFS). In seven of those cases, flight operations at the airport were temporarily suspended.

This is an jump from last year, when eight drones were detected at the airport and its surroundings in the whole of 2025, according to DFS.

This is a developing story. Please refresh for updates.

entries.title: Harvey Weinstein resentenced to 15 years for sexual assault
entries.summary: The disgraced Hollywood mogul was found guilty of sexually assaulting former production assistant Miriam Haley. The man whose case spurred the #MeToo movement awaits a separate sentencing in a California rape case.
entries.content:
September 23, 2026

The disgraced Hollywood mogul was found guilty of sexually assaulting former production assistant Miriam Haley. The man whose case spurred the #MeToo movement awaits a separate sentencing in a California rape case.

Disgraced movie mogul Harvey Weinstein was resentenced on Wednesday to 15 years in prison for sexually assaulting former production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006.

Once one of Hollywood's most powerful kingpins, churning out hits such as "Pulp Fiction", "Shakespeare in Love" and "Chocolat," Weinstein's fall from grace came when sexual assault allegations compounded against him in 2017, spiraling into Hollywood's #MeToo movement.

Accounts of several women who worked with him across the years showed a pattern of abusing his power in Hollywood and ability to make or break careers to extract sexual favors and sexually assault women.

What do we know about Haley's case?

Weinstein was found guilty of forcibly performing oral sex on Haley in 2006.

The former producer said she had accepted an invitation to his Manhattan apartment when he lunged to kiss her, and though she rebuffed him, he grabbed her and sexually assaulted her, ignoring her pleas to stop.

Weinstein was sentenced in 2020 to 23 years for the sexual assault of Haley, but the sentence was overturned in 2024 on appeal. A jury found him guilty again in 2025.

What happened in court?

On Wednesday, a 74-year-old, wheelchair-bound Weinstein made an appeal for leniency, apologizing to those he may have hurt.

"I do have remorse for Miriam Haley's pain, but I have to reiterate my innocence," he told the judge.

Haley stressed the assault was akin to "a life sentence."

"Having been sexually assaulted by Harvey Weinstein has had a devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away. Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come," she said.

Prosecutors had sought a 20-year sentence for the disgraced producer, but his lawyers warned that a longer sentence would likely see him die in prison.

What other cases await Weinstein in court?

Weinstein also awaits a resentencing in a separate rape and assault case in California, where he is accused of assaulting an actress in a Los Angeles hotel room in 2013. In June, an appeals court upheld his conviction but scrapped his 16-year prison term.

Meanwhile, prosecutors said they will not pursue a fourth trial in the case of him sexually assaulting actor Jessica Mann.

In May, a New York judge declared a mistrial after the jury failed to reach a verdict. It was the third time Mann had taken the stand against Weinstein and she said she could not bear to testify again.

Another 2020 verdict for Weinstein in the Mann case was overturned due to mishandling of witnesses, and a 2025 case ended in mistrial.

Weinstein's lawyers have called for leniency, arguing their client is in failing health as he battles blood cancer, congestive heart failure and kidney issues.

entries.title: New fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region raises fears of a return to the country's civil war
entries.summary: Fighting in and around Tigray is testing Ethiopia's fragile 2022 peace deal. With old enemies forming new alliances, experts warn that the conflict could enter a dangerous new phase.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Ethiopia: Where does the Tigray conflict go from here?

September 23, 2026

Fighting in and around Tigray is testing Ethiopia's fragile 2022 peace deal. With old enemies forming new alliances, experts warn that the conflict could enter a dangerous new phase.

The fighting reported in and around Ethiopia's northern Tigray region marks more than another episode of tension between the federal government in Addis Ababa and the region's leadership. It raises a fundamental question: What remains of the fragile peace established in 2022 — and where does the conflict go from here?

From 2020 to 2022, Ethiopia was devastated by a civil war between the federal government in Addis Ababa and Tigray's regional leadership. The conflict drew in neighboring regions and foreign troops from Eritrea, leading to a humanitarian crisis that displaced millions and left hundreds of thousands dead.

While a peace agreement halted the worst of the bloodshed in late 2022, it left a lot of the political and territorial disputes unresolved.

DW spoke to witnesses in the towns of Abala and Erebti on the border with Tigray who confirmed that new fighting had taken place there between Tigray forces and Ethiopian federal troops. Humanitarian sources also reported clashes in the area. Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to the cities of Mekelle, Shire and Axum, citing the "current situation in the Tigray region."

Reports that Tigray forces have taken control of airports in the region could not independently be verified by DW.

For Oslo-based peace researcher Kjetil Tronvoll, however, the latest developments represent a decisive escalation.

"I think the war has already begun," Tronvoll told DW.

German security analyst Gerrit Kurtz of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin also sees the developments as a serious escalation.

"This is a step towards a war," he told DW.

Two competing narratives

The two sides are presenting fundamentally different accounts of what triggered the latest escalation.

In a statement issued on September 23, the National Regional Government of Tigray said its forces had been responding defensively to an attack by the federal government. It accused Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of launching a new "genocidal invasion" and said Tigray forces had been ordered to defend the population.

The Tigray government also accused Addis Ababa of carrying out air and drone strikes and artillery attacks in recent months. It said it had previously refrained from responding to what it described as repeated provocations in an effort to de-escalate the situation.

The allegations could not independently be verified. The federal government, meanwhile, has portrayed the developments as part of a broader coordinated threat involving armed groups opposed to the prime minister.

The competing narratives illustrate one of the central problems facing any renewed peace effort: The parties do not even agree on the basic interpretation of the escalation.

A fragile peace under pressure

The current crisis cannot be separated from the shortcomings of the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. The deal ended two years of devastating war between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), but it did not resolve some of the conflict's underlying political and territorial disputes.

Western Tigray remains particularly contentious. The return of hundreds of thousands of displaced people remains unresolved, while questions over Tigray's political representation and its relationship with the federal government continue to fuel tensions.

"The Pretoria agreement stopped the fighting, but it did not resolve the underlying political conflict," Tronvoll says.

At the heart of that conflict is a fundamental disagreement over Ethiopia's political order. The TPLF has traditionally defended a strong federal structure and substantial regional autonomy. Abiy Ahmed's government has pursued a more centralized political model.

The issue is therefore not simply whether individual provisions of the peace agreement are implemented. It is also about competing visions of how Ethiopia should be governed.

Former enemies join forces

The emergence of an alliance of seven armed groups opposing Abiy adds another layer of complexity.

The grouping includes the TPLF, Fano forces from the state of Amhara and the Oromo Liberation Army from another regional state within Ethiopia. Some of these organizations were bitter enemies during the Tigray war. Their decision to cooperate therefore represents a significant political development — but not necessarily a durable alliance.

Kurtz says the alliance has been developing for some time and that some of its leaders have apparently already met.

"It was a very important development," he says. "The alliance has been in the making for a long time."

At the same time, he points to the fundamental differences between its members.

"All the political differences that they have are certainly there to resolve once their overall joint aim is achieved, which is overthrowing the government of Abiy."

Tronvoll similarly describes the cooperation as primarily tactical. The question is whether the groups can turn their shared opposition to Abiy into a lasting political and military strategy.

There is another complicating factor: Eritrea.

The Ethiopian government has accused neighboring Eritrea of supporting the alliance. Eritrea has rejected such allegations. Kurtz says there have been reports of contacts between the armed groups and Eritrea, but stresses that the new alliance itself appears to be a domestic grouping.

The geography of the alliance is another obstacle. Its members operate in different parts of Ethiopia and pursue different political objectives. Coordinating military operations across such distances would be difficult.

Can the escalation still be contained?

The most urgent question is whether the current fighting can still be contained before it develops into another full-scale war.

Kurtz argues that the immediate priority is straightforward: The forces involved in the fighting need to stop.

"Both the Ethiopian armed forces as well as the Tigray security forces are involved in active hostilities right now. So they should stop this," he says.

But bringing the fighting to an end will require more than a ceasefire on the ground. Ethiopia's conflict has become increasingly fragmented. Armed groups are operating not only in Tigray, but also in Amhara and Oromia, two other regional states within Ethiopia. Regional actors such as Eritrea are potentially also playing a role.

Who can mediate?

International actors have repeatedly warned about the risk of renewed conflict. Yet sustained diplomatic engagement has so far failed to produce a new political process.

The United States remains an important actor, according to Kurtz, but he says Washington has not shown sufficient engagement. The African Union, the European Union and other international actors could also play a role.

The challenge is that there is no single actor with enough influence over all the parties.

"It will require a certain coalition of efforts," Kurtz says. He argues that preventing a wider war would require a broader diplomatic push, with international actors dividing responsibilities and coordinating their efforts.

The United Nations General Assembly in New York could provide an opportunity for international leaders to engage directly with the Ethiopian government, he says. But diplomacy would also have to address the armed groups involved in the new alliance.

Tronvoll is similarly critical of the international response so far. He argues that the warning signs had been visible for some time but that international efforts to bring the parties back to negotiations remained limited.

The political problem remains

For the people of Tigray, the stakes are particularly high. The region has yet to recover from the consequences of the 2020-2022 war. Many people remain displaced, infrastructure has been severely damaged and the economic recovery remains fragile.

A return to large-scale war would therefore not simply mean a resumption of an old conflict. It could open a new and potentially broader phase of Ethiopia's wider security crisis, particularly given the simultaneous conflicts in Amhara and Oromia.

The immediate priority is to prevent the latest fighting from developing into a wider war. But any sustainable settlement will have to address the political questions that the 2022 agreement left unresolved.

The key question is therefore not simply whether the war has returned.

It is whether Ethiopia and its international partners can still create enough diplomatic space to prevent the latest escalation from closing the door to a political solution.

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

entries.title: Eviction of 87-year-old woman sparks housing protests in Madrid
entries.summary: Police escorted Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had called home for more than seven decades. The case has reignited debate over Spain's housing crisis, rising rents and protections for long-term tenants.
entries.content:
Spain

Eviction of 87-year-old woman sparks protests in Madrid

September 23, 2026

Police escorted Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had called home for more than seven decades. The case has reignited debate over Spain's housing crisis, rising rents and protections for long-term tenants.

The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman sparked protests in the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday.

Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her residence on Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street, where she had lived for at least 70 years of her life.

"I have lived here for 71 years and I don't want to leave," Maricarmen told reporters as the eviction was being carried out.

Dozens of people protested behind the police cordon, chanting, "Maricarmen, you are not alone" and "Murderers!"

The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent.

With only 30 minutes to gather her belongings, Maricarmen was escorted by riot police officers. She was removed from her home on a stretcher and taken to an ambulance.

An 8-year-long battle

Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, when a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.

According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company has lasted eight years, and this was the fourth attempt to evict her from the home.

The elderly woman's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said that the real estate company had rejected proposals from the legal team as well as requests to postpone her removal from the property.

The company has not made any public statements on the matter.

Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for Inquilinas de Madrid, a tenants' association that seeks to combat what it describes as the "rental bubble" in the Madrid region, said that Maricarmen was taken by ambulance to a local hospital.

She also announced that a writer, who wishes to remain anonymous, had offered to pay the elderly woman's rent, but the real estate company rejected the proposal.

Spain's housing crisis

Spain remains divided over how to address the worsening housing crisis.

The country's left-wing coalition government has pushed for stronger tenant protections and broader rent controls. However, it argues that as long as Parliament remains divided, it will be difficult to pass such measures.

Meanwhile, Madrid's regional government, led by the conservative People's Party, has favored a more market-oriented approach.

The president of the Community of Madrid, Isabel Diaz Ayuso, is currently embroiled in a controversy related to the purchase of luxury properties valued at €6.3 million ($7.2 million).

entries.title: Trump's Board of Peace proposes $2.45B for reconstruction in Gaza
entries.summary: The board has noted that the Palestinian enclave needs roughly $35.2 billion for full, medium-term reconstruction. Trump's plan for peace in Gaza has largely stalled since an agreement was reached almost a year ago.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

Trump's Board of Peace proposes $2.45B to rebuild Gaza

September 23, 2026

The board has noted that the Palestinian enclave needs roughly $35.2 billion for full, medium-term reconstruction. Trump's plan for peace in Gaza has largely stalled since an agreement was reached almost a year ago.

US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has proposed a six-month plan for the reconstruction and governance of the Palestinian Gaza Strip, costing some $2.45 billion (roughly €2.15 billion).

The plan was unveiled during a meeting on Wednesday.

It involves a 66-project blueprint to kick things off, but acknowledges the enormous hurdles that must be overcome to rebuild the devastated enclave, where last October's ceasefire has only slowed Israeli attacks.

What do we know about the Board of Peace Gaza reconstruction plans?

Former UK prime minister Tony Blair, who serves on the organization's executive board, said that Palestinians in Gaza "don't need a slogan; they need a solution."

The reconstruction and governance projects include estimated spending for:

  • Temporary housing
  • Rubble removal
  • Hospital repairs
  • Economic recovery
  • Deployment of a multinational security force

The initiatives are all designed to support Trump's 20-point plan to end the war.

"The need is immense," the board said, estimating that full reconstruction will cost roughly $35.2 billion over the medium term and another $71.4 billion in the next decade.

The proposal also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects, as per an Axios report released ahead of the meeting.

Where do things stand in Gaza now?

Trump's Gaza peace plan, which ushered in the October 10 ceasefire last year, included:

  • Additional Israeli military withdrawals from Gaza
  • The disarmament of the Palestinian militant group Hamas
  • The arrival of an international peacekeeping force
  • A new apolitical Palestinian government to administer the territory's day-to-day business

However, almost a year on, completion of the plan has remained elusive..

Israel still occupies roughly 60% of the territory and regularly carries out deadly attacks it says target Hamas militants. Gaza health authorities say over 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed since the ceasefire. The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed.

Hamas, designated as a terrorist group by several countries, has thus far not given up its weapons, despite on some occasions expressing its readiness to do so. Israel has said it will not withdraw from areas it occupies until the group fully disarms and is removed from the enclave.

Meanwhile, most Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homes, with no international military force or new government materializing.

The Board of Peace's high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, has said that progress relies heavily on Hamas disarming, but he has also called on Israel to scale back its military operations.

entries.title: Who is skipping the UN General Assembly — and why
entries.summary: Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, Friedrich Merz, Giorgia Meloni and Mahmoud Abbas are among more than 50 leaders who won't make it to the UN General Assembly. Their reasons range from illness and domestic affairs to holidays.
entries.content:
September 23, 2026

Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, Friedrich Merz, Giorgia Meloni and Mahmoud Abbas are among more than 50 leaders who won't make it to the UN General Assembly. Their reasons range from illness and domestic affairs to holidays.

Few world leaders would miss a stage like the United Nations General Assembly. Donald Trump, Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Emmanuel Macron are among those in New York for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly — or UNGA81 for short — where the speeches from the green marble lectern make headlines around the globe. 

That makes the no-shows all the more surprising. Here is a look at some of the leaders staying away — and why.

Germany: Friedrich Merz

The German chancellor, in his second year in office, would like to be much more present on the international stage and has described himself as a  "foreign-policy chancellor." But domestic politics have been keeping him busy. Three German states held parliamentary elections in September and Friedrich Merz is under more pressure as chancellor and leader of the Christian Democrats (CDU) than ever before. In Saxony-Anhalt and Berlin, the CDU was firmly voted out of office, while in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern it failed to enter the state parliament at all — a first since the founding of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Merz is in crisis-management mode at home and seems to want to prevent his opponents from planning a revolt in his absence. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul will speak in his place.

Italy: Giorgia Meloni

Italy's prime minister is in a considerably stronger position than Merz but has said she needs to deal with domestic matters this week. After the NATO summit in early July, Giorgia Meloni said she had just returned from several international summits and had to tackle various issues, including some pending within Italy. She pointed out that Merz had also been absent in 2025 - she too is sending her foreign minister, Antonio Tajani.

South Africa: Cyril Ramaphosa

The South African president has also just attended an international summit — the BRICS summit in India. He said he would not attend the UN General Assembly for health reasons: medics advised him to take time to rest and recover. His office did not disclose details about his condition. South Africa will also be represented at the UN lectern by Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.

Egypt: Abdel Fattah al-Sisi

Along with Africa's largest economy, the second- and third-largest economies on the continent are also not sending their presidents to New York: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is being represented by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly. Al-Sisi's office did not give a reason for his absence. During his first years in office, from 2014 onward, he regularly attended the UN General Assembly. In 2020, the event was held online because of the coronavirus pandemic and the following year it was a hybrid event, to which al-Sisi sent a pre-recorded video message. He has not attended since the General Assembly returned to in-person meetings.

Nigeria: Bola Tinubu

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu is the third influential African leader to miss this year's UN General Assembly. His spokesman was quoted by Nigerian media as saying the West African country would be "fully and effectively represented" by Vice President Kashim Shettima. Tinubu, meanwhile, is on vacation: He spent time in the UK in late August before traveling to France.

India: Narendra Modi

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is relatively rarely to be seen at UN General Assemblies. He last took the podium in 2021, since when the world's largest democracy has consistently sent Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar instead. According to Indian media outlets, Modi was reportedly listed as a speaker at this year's gathering before his plans changed. Why he decided not to attend is not known.

China: Xi Jinping

Chinese President Xi Jinping's absence is under international scrutiny this year. As this year's "High-Level Week" takes place, Xi will also be in the US but he will not be going to New York. Instead, he will head straight for Washington, some 300 kilometers away, for a full state visit, including a White House gala dinner and a military parade.

Although Beijing has not framed it this way, the timing suggests that Xi is prioritizing great power diplomacy over the United Nations' multilateral forum. Xi and Trump have serious bones of contention, including over trade relations, artificial intelligence and Taiwan's security situation.

Russia: Vladimir Putin

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also rarely stood at the iconic podium so it comes as little surprise that Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will once again speak for Russia this year. Putin ordered this by decree — and didn't offer a reason for his absence.

Palestinian territories: Mahmoud Abbas

Mahmoud Abbashas clocked up far more UNGA experience than any of those listed above. The president of the Palestinian Authority (PA), who has been in office since 2005, was a regular until Donald Trump's second term.

But last year, the Trump administration denied him a diplomatic visa and has done so again this year.

Yet, under the 1947 UN Headquarters Agreement, the United States is committed to facilitating access to UN headquarters for foreign representatives. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, for example, is still due to speak in New York, despite the US having recently bombed Iran.

In the case of the Palestinians, the US State Department recently said it was extending sanctions "that deny visas to members of the Palestine Liberation Organization and the Palestinian Authority." Abbas plans to address the assembled heads of state and government by video message, as he did last year.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Could a Left Party government in Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?
entries.summary: The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election partly on the promise to implement the city's 2021 expropriation referendum as a way to solve the city's rent crisis. But can it really happen?
entries.content:
Germany

Could Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?

September 23, 2026

The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election partly on the promise to implement the city's 2021 expropriation referendum as a way to solve the city's rent crisis. But can it really happen?

The socialist Left Party, which won the Berlin election on September 20, was the only major party on the ballot that said it would implement the results of Berlin's 2021 referendum, when 57.6% of Berliners voted to expropriate the apartments owned by real estate companies that own more than 3,000 units.

But the federal government has said they won't let it happen. So is it even possible? And how did we get here? DW explains:

  • What did the Left Party say about expropriation?

The Left Party was one of the main supporters of a successful, years-long grassroots campaign called "Deutsche Wohnen & Co. enteignen," ("Expropriate Deutsche Wohnen").

Deutsche Wohnen is a major property developer that owns over 140,000 units across Germany, and 100,000 in Berlin alone.

The campaign and the Left Party argued that by expropriating this and a handful of other major companies like it, the Berlin government could put some 270,000 apartments in Berlin into public ownership, and make them available at affordable rent prices. Other estimates put the number at around 240,000.

The argument struck a chord, as surveys showed that housing and rent prices were the biggest concerns for Berlin voters in the recent election.

Some 25% of rented property in Berlin is already in public ownership, through state-owned companies like Berlinovo. The expropriation measure would likely push that up to over 30%.

  • The 2021 referendum — what was the question and what came out of it?

The original referendum, held in September 2021, asked Berliners to vote yes or no on a five-point plan:

- Socializing the apartments owned by the major property companies

- Administration of the properties by a public-law entity

- Administration of the properties with participation from both city officials, renters, and local communities

- Ban on any re-privatization

- Compensation for the property companies "significantly below" the market value of the property

The referendum did not oblige the state government — at the time a coalition of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the Greens, and the Left Party — to immediately implement the plan. 

Instead, the then-SPD Mayor Franziska Giffey put together a 13-person expert commission, including former justice ministers and constitutional law experts. This was given the task of establishing whether the plan conformed with the German constitution, or Basic Law, and how the compensation could be organized.

In 2023, the commission concluded that expropriation was legal and possible, though budget questions still needed to be clarified.

By then, a new conservative-led government, headed by the Christian Democratic Union's (CDU) Kai Wegner, had been voted into office, and announced that it would not expropriate any real estate companies, regardless of what the commission said. At the same time, it emerged that the Berlin CDU was receiving hundreds of thousands of euros in donations from property companies.

Instead, the government said it would draw up a socialization law that would define the conditions for the socialization of property, while ruling out expropriation. A draft law was completed in December 2025.

The Deutsche Wohnen Enteignen campaign rejected this idea as pointless, and had in the meantime gathered legal experts to draw up its own expropriation and socialization law, and promised to start another campaign to force a referendum to implement that.

  • The legal basis for expropriation: Articles 14 and 15 of the German constitution

The original campaign founded its plan on articles 14 and 15 of the German Basic Law.

Article 14 says that, while the right to property is guaranteed, "expropriation shall only be permissible for the public good."

Article 15 states: "Land, natural resources and means of production may, for the purpose of nationalization, be transferred to public ownership or other forms of public enterprise by a law that determines the nature and extent of compensation."

As far as the campaigners are concerned, the law they have drawn up covers those two bases.

But, while Article 14 is implemented often enough (for example, when the state wants to build a new highway), Article 15 has never been implemented at all. It is new legal territory, and no one is quite sure what would happen if it were tried.

Some legal experts say the plan would contravene European law. Housing companies would almost certainly fight the measure in court and demand more compensation than the government is willing to offer.

  • 'Not happening' — Chancellor Merz vows to prevent expropriation

Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded to the Left Party's election victory immediately by promising to draw up a federal law banning state governments from expropriating property. 

"It's not just about banning something here in Berlin," Merz said at a press conference in the aftermath of the Berlin election. "It's about sending a clear message to international investors, which is: There is no expropriation of private property in Germany."

However, it's unclear whether the federal government has the power to impose such a law. Germany's Constitutional Court once ruled that the federal government cannot pass a law simply to prevent a state from governing in the issues it wants.

  • What now?

The Left Party still has to enter into coalition negotiations to form a government in Berlin. Its most likely coalition partners are the SPD and the Greens, and given the opposition from the federal government and the massive controversy over the issue, the expropriation plan could become a major sticking point.

Whatever happens, the Left Party itself acknowledges that expropriation and socialization would take a while to put into practice, and it would be even longer before it had a measurable effect on Berlin's overall rents.

In the meantime, it has drawn up a number of laws that it hopes will tackle the problem more quickly, such as a rent cap.

In any case, Berliners themselves appear to have gone a little cold on the idea. Despite the Left's electoral success, a recent poll by infratest-dimap found that only 37% of Berliners are still in favor of expropriating real estate companies.

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

entries.title: China's 13-year-old swimming star raises questions on child athletes
entries.summary: Three gold medals and three Asian Games records have catapulted China's Yu Zidi, 13, into the sporting spotlight. She is far from the first teen prodigy, but should teens be competing at elite level?
entries.content:
September 23, 2026

Three gold medals and three Asian Games records have catapulted China's Yu Zidi, 13, into the sporting spotlight. She is far from the first teen prodigy, but should teens be competing at elite level?

The third Asian Games gold medal looked as convincing as the first two, even if Yu Zidi insisted that: "It didn't feel easy at all. It was quite challenging."

On Wednesday, the 13-year-old Chinese swimmer broke the Games record for the third time to add the women's 400 meter individual medley title to her golds in the 200 meter medley and 200 meter butterfly. The three medals add to a bronze she won last year at the World Championships.

Even two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics, talk is turning to a potential rivalry with Canada's Summer McIntosh, 20, who herself finished fourth in the 2020 Olympics at 14 and won a world title at 15. As well as their remarkable talent, the pair's youth has raised some questions.

"The first reaction you have when you see something like this is you think, wow, there's a big career ahead," three-time open water swimming world champion Leonie Beck, of Germany, told DW.

"But I think maybe this is the problem. People around [the athlete], or maybe the media can create this pressure on a young talent. But just because you're really good and fast at this age, doesn't mean that your whole career will continue like this."

Early success is not always sustained

Beck has already retired from elite competition at 29 and swimming is a sport where athletes often peak early. Katie Ledecky, of the US, and Japan's Kyoko Iwasaki both won Olympic gold at 15 and Japan's Yumeki Kojima, 17, has been a home favorite at the Asian Games, winning a gold and silver in the pool.

While the temptation is to think of Yu as a prodigy, Beck said that to reach the level she has also requires extraordinary dedication and sacrifice.

"My first international competition was in 2011 [at age 14]. At that stage already, I was training eight times a week. You wake up at 5 a.m., by 6 you're in the pool, out at 7:30 so you're in school at 8:00, school until 1, going home, eating, maybe doing some homework, going back in the water training at 3. Then one hour of dry land [training], then in the water again and coming back home at 7 (p.m.). I had this when I was young too."

Yu, who was discovered by chance by a swimming coach at a water park aged 6, admitted in an interview with state media Xinhua at an event in China in January that the workload takes its toll.

"Being in class all day and still having to train was really tiring," she said. "Sometimes I was so tired I could fall asleep even while eating."

While, for Beck, the sporting success made such struggles worthwhile, not all athletes who dedicate their childhoods to their sport reach the pinnacle. The German swimmer added that putting educational, physical and mental support structures in place is critical for sports that allow under-18s to compete.

"Sport psychology should start at a really young age because it should be normal, the same as physiotherapists," she said. "Especially at a young age, where sport should be also fun."

World Aquatics rules state that the minimum age for international championships is 14 but exceptions can be made for those fast enough, like Yu. While swimmers peak earlier than athletes in other sports, teenagers at the top level are not so unusual.

In football, Lamine Yamal won the Euros with Spain at 16, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, of India, made his debut in cricket's Indian Premier League at 13 and Nadia Comaneci, of Romania, became the first gymnast to be awarded a perfect 10 in the 1976 Olympics in Montreal aged 14.

Neither are young athletes a modern phenomenon. Dimitrios Loundras remains the youngest ever Olympic medallist, winning a bronze with the Greek gymnastics team in 1896.

While support structures in sport are improving, challenges remain, according to Rosemary Purcell, who played a part in the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) review into youth development ahead of the Paris Olympics in 2024.

"There are pretty stark differences between what we see in the community and in these elite youth athletes," Purcell told DW during those Games.

"Some sports do have a higher rate of eating disorders and body image disturbance in young athletes, but conversely, they may have lower rates of depression and anxiety than we would see in the community."

If you're good enough, you're old enough?

In general, sporting bodies tend to take the approach that if an athlete is good enough, they are old enough. Beck said, allied with the right support, this approach is correct.

"Every athlete has completely different development. Why should you take away the success of a young athlete just because she's young and successful in that age? In my opinion, you should give her the possibility to be successful at that age because maybe, who knows, in a later stage of her career, she will be not that successful. It's not just a solution to say: 'look, you're that age, you're not able to compete.'"

But she also cautioned that because success won't always last, young elite sportspeople should be helped to find a plan away from the pitch, pool or mat, something she struggled somewhat with post Paris 2024.

"You have this idea that, ok, I want to reach the Olympic Games, win this medal. So you have a structure of where to go, what to do. And at one point it's gone and you're like, ‘ok, but now what am I doing with my life? What do I want to reach? What are my goals?'

"It's really, really important that people are starting to think that, 'hey, we are also human beings and you should do something to have a life after the sport because the sport is not endless.'"

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Pakistan's jailed former PM Khan's sons told DW the authorities are cracking down ahead of new PTI protests
entries.summary: The sons of jailed Pakistani ex-PM Imran Khan told DW their father is in ill health while being isolated from family and doctors. Other relatives have been detained ahead of a planned opposition protest.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan: Khan family arrests raise stakes ahead of protests

September 23, 2026

The sons of jailed Pakistani ex-PM Imran Khan told DW their father is in ill health while being isolated from family and doctors. Other relatives have been detained ahead of a planned opposition protest.

Family members of Pakistan's former Prime Minister Imran Khan are concerned about the 73-year-old's health in a Rawalpindi prison and accuse authorities of preventing him from accessing appropriate medical care.

Khan's London-based sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, told DW they had received "little to no information" about their father's health.

"When we last spoke to him on the phone back in March, he said that he had lost 85% of the vision in his right eye and that despite his complaints, it was neglected for months," they said.

The brothers added that their father was being held in a tiny cell and has been allowed outside for only one or two hours a day. They also allege that he was kept in isolation from family, lawyers, and a personal physician for 10 months before he was briefly allowed to see two of his sisters.

Meanwhile, the opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party's has planned a protest march on September 27 to exert pressure on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's government for Khan's release.

Sons demand family access and medical care for Khan

Khan's sons have urged authorities to allow their father access to a personal physician and to restore regular access to his family and phone calls.

"We are asking the Pakistani authorities to obey the Supreme Court orders immediately and shift our father to Shifa International Hospital so that he can be assessed by independent doctors," they said.



Khan's sisters detained as PTI plans new protests

From jail, Khan remains at the center of Pakistan's political confrontation between the PTI and the country's powerful military. He remains a popular political figure in Pakistan, despite being ousted from office in 2022  a parliamentary no-confidence vote.

Khan's three sisters were detained in the Punjab capital of Lahore on Monday ahead of the planned PTI protest march.

The detention orders cited concerns that the sisters were a threat to public safety and maintenance of public order. All three were ordered to be held for 30 days under a public order ordinance.

Khan's sons told DW the arrests were intended to intimidate their family and supporters before the planned protest rally.

"Our family members who have been arbitrarily taken into custody must be released immediately," they said. "The abductions of our family members in the middle of the night, with no reason given, were purely to intimidate them."

Khan was ousted as prime minister in 2022 and jailed the following year on what he says are politically motivated corruption charges. His PTI party says it has faced an ongoing government crackdown.

Pakistan government calls for 'order'

Pakistan's government rejected these claims and said that its priority was to maintain public order during the planned protest.

Authorities have stepped up security preparations in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, deploying thousands of police personnel and placing shipping containers and other barriers at key entry points.

Talal Chaudhary, Pakistan's minister of state for interior, warned that the government would not tolerate unlawful activity or actions threatening lives and property.

"If you are a peaceful citizen, come to Islamabad from any route, come 100 times," he told DW. "But if you come as terrorists, we will not let you leave."

In 2024, pro-Khan protests on the streets of Islamabad turned violent. Demonstrators breached high security zones and clashes with security forces left six dead. When Khan was arrested in May 2023, nationwide PTI support rallies also led to violence, with military and government buildings suffering damage. Several people were killed and hundreds injured.

"The right to protest does not give the right to attack," Chaudhary said.

Arrests could 'galvanize' PTI supporters

The PTI has said the September 27 protest will call for respect for constitutional and political rights.

Michael Kugelman, a South Asia analyst at the Washington-based Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, told DW that the arrests would likely further energize Khan's supporters.

"The arrests will galvanize what is already an angry and anxious Khan support base," he said.

He added that the detention of Khan's sisters, who Kugelman said were"prominent advocates" of Khan's cause had placed his family at the center of the confrontation between the government and the PTI.

Khan's base is "concerned about the state of his health, and for his sister to be detained will increase the chance that protesters take to the streets on the 27th," he added.

Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader and close aide to Khan, said the arrests were meant to create fear but would not prevent the party from mobilizing its supporters across the country.

"What they [the government] don't realize is all they are doing is creating more hatred for themselves among the public," he told DW.

Bukhari described the current repression as the most severe the PTI has faced. "This crackdown seems the more brutal," he said, adding that the government was acting out of frustration.

"They are fueling a fire that will soon be out of their control," he asserted. "They can keep attacking us, and we will continue to resist. This protest will go on, and many more after it," he added.

As Pakistan's government faces several challenges, including economic malaise, conflict with the Afghan Taliban, and fallout from the Iran war, further domestic unrest would be an unwelcome complication.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Slovakia: PM Robert Fico's NATO Article 5 remarks spark criticism and raise questions about his country's NATO commitment
entries.summary: Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico says he fears war and will do everything he can to keep his country out of one. Critics say his remarks risk weakening NATO, the alliance that was designed to prevent such a war.
entries.content:
Slovakia

Slovakia's Fico draws fire over NATO Article 5 remarks

September 23, 2026

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico says he fears war and will do everything he can to keep his country out of one. Critics say his remarks risk weakening NATO, the alliance that was designed to prevent such a war.

"I'm afraid of war," Robert Fico told medical students at a teaching hospital in Presov last week.

"What is happening in Europe today, what we're hearing and seeing today, is that the military conflict in Ukraine has got out of control," he went on, warning them that Europe faced the possibility of a wider war.

He asked the students to imagine Slovakia being told to prepare "5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers" who would go somewhere to fight "without us even knowing whom they are fighting, or why, or what for."

Then he turned to Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

"I do not want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5," Fico said.

"Yes, we are in NATO. We value that. Cooperation and fulfilling our obligations matter to us. But as prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a military conflict."

The remarks prompted uproar from the Slovak opposition and also a spat with Petr Pavel, president of neighboring Czechia and former chairman of NATO's Military Committee.

"If anyone says they're glad to be a member of NATO … but are unwilling to get involved if anyone else is attacked, then they have not understood the word solidarity," Pavel said.

Fico replied that he understood that Pavel, as a former NATO general, would like to fight, while he himself preferred peace.

The impact on Slovakia's standing

The Slovak prime minister's fear of a wider war is shared by many Europeans. But critics at home gave his remarks short shrift.

"Isn't he a prime minister? Isn't he the leader of a country? Is he not supposed to lead people instead of expressing fears?" asked former Slovak Foreign Minister Miro Wlachovsky, now a distinguished fellow at the GLOBSEC think tank.

"My question for him as prime minister is: OK, even if the situation is as bad as you are saying, what I want to hear from you is how the country is prepared. What have you done for preparedness? Who will come to our aid in case we are attacked?" Wlachovsky told DW.

Asked whether Fico's remarks could damage Slovakia's standing among its allies, Wlachovsky replied: "It's already done."

Political background to Fico's comments

Analysts see a clear political context to Fico's remarks.

The Slovak prime minister will face a difficult reelection fight next year. Some observers believe Fico is trying to steal votes from the extreme-right Republika party, which is viscerally hostile to NATO and the EU and opposes military support for Ukraine.

Wlachovsky compared Fico's rhetoric to that of Hungary's former Prime Minister Viktor Orban and the current Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, both of whom have presented themselves as the candidates of peace.

Babis was heavily criticized during his unsuccessful 2023 presidential campaign after questioning during a televised debate whether the Czech Republic should send troops to NATO ally Poland if it came under attack.

What is NATO's Article 5?

Oana Lungescu, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute and a former NATO spokesperson, told DW that Article 5 was "the most solemn pledge that a country can make to another."

But its central purpose, she said, was deterrence: convincing a potential aggressor that it would face the alliance together, rather than an isolated member.

"This is about solidarity, standing together, underpinning deterrence and therefore avoiding war," she said. "NATO is a defensive alliance. It's not an offensive alliance."

Nor would invoking Article 5 automatically send every member's troops into combat, she said.

The North Atlantic Council, where every ally is represented, would assess an attack and decide by consensus whether it constituted an Article 5 situation — Slovakia's voice would be equal to that of its 31 partners in that room, she said.

Once consensus was reached, each country would then assist the attacked ally by taking the action it deemed necessary, which might — or might not — involve armed force.

Article 5 has been invoked only once, following the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.

Lungescu pointed to one of NATO's initial responses: sending AWACS surveillance aircraft to patrol US skies and help prevent another attack.

She pointed out that Slovakia already benefits from the same solidarity Fico appeared to question. The country hosts a NATO multinational battlegroup established after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with personnel from several allies alongside Slovak troops.

Its purpose is to deter an attack on Slovakia.

'Exactly what Putin wants'

For former Slovak Defense Minister Jaroslav Nad, the danger lies in allowing that fear to dictate policy towards Ukraine.

"This is exactly what Vladimir Putin wants," said Nad, who was defense minister from 2020 to 2023 and is now head of the non-parliamentary opposition Democrats party.

"He wants citizens in the EU and NATO to believe that if EU and NATO countries continue to support Ukraine, this escalatory situation might lead to a Third World War or something like that," Nad told DW.

Nad was in office when Slovakia decided to hand over its entire fleet of ageing MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine. Fico's government later sought a criminal investigation into the transfer; prosecutors closed the case, finding no crime.

"Even when I was defense minister, I heard this not only from ordinary people but also from some ministers around the table: that we shouldn't help Ukraine with this or that equipment or capability or ammunition, because it might create a difficult situation in terms of escalation towards Russia," he went on.

"None of that happened."

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
